I read Cisco's v2.0 outline in full and could not find QoS, policing, shaping or queuing in it. Cisco says its topic list is a guide and related topics may still appear, so a topic missing from the outline is not a promise. Still:
if you sit v1.1 (before 3 February 2027), study this chapter properly. If you sit v2.0, treat it as background knowledge

and give your time to the topics the v2.0 outline lists. Check the Cisco Learning Network page for the date rule that applies to you. I believe v1.1 kept objective 4.7, but I could not open Cisco's own v1.1 PDF.

C - CoS is a 3-bit Layer 2 marking (PCP in a VLAN tag). DSCP, IP precedence and ToS are Layer 3.
How many bits are in DSCP, and in which header?
6 bits, inside the 8-bit DS field of the IP header - the other 2 bits are ECN.
Which advanced tool classifies applications by looking deep into the payload?
A - NBAR does Layer 4-7 deep-packet inspection.
What DSCP value is EF, and what traffic normally uses it?
46; voice - EF gives low loss, low latency, low jitter.

The book calls WFQ "the Cisco default". As far as I know, the default depends on the interface speed (WFQ on slow serial interfaces, FIFO on fast interfaces). I did not verify this in this session, so for the exam use the book's statement.
The two modern methods: CBWFQ and LLQ (book pp. 459-460)
Take the priority queue away from LLQ and you are left with CBWFQ, which the book says is only used for data-traffic networks.
Exam Essentials: the two queuing mechanisms you should use today are
. Know the starvation problem with strict priority and why round-robin hurts real-time traffic.
What is queue starvation, and which scheduling method can cause it?
Low-priority queues never get served; strict priority scheduling - strict priority only serves lower queues when higher queues are empty.
Which queuing mechanism provides both bandwidth and latency guarantees for voice and data?
D - LLQ adds a strict-priority queue to CBWFQ.
Does scheduling happen only during congestion?
No. Queuing is activated by congestion; scheduling always runs - scheduling decides the next packet out of the interface.
TCP's sliding windows give flow control. When loss occurs TCP cuts its sending rate sharply, then speeds up again once things clear. That behaviour causes problems on busy links:
because the queue is full. It wastes bandwidth, because TCP just resends the data.

Which of these is a congestion-avoidance mechanism?
B - WRED drops packets early, weighted by priority.
Many TCP senders slow down and speed up together after loss, so bandwidth is used in waves and partly wasted - WRED avoids it by dropping packets early at different times.

A user complains that voice calls break up only during large file transfers. Which change best helps?
B. Add an LLQ priority queue for voice marked EF
D. Use a policer on voice
B - LLQ gives voice a strict-priority queue with low latency.
A. Policers delay traffic, shapers drop it
B. Shapers delay traffic, policers drop or re-mark it
B - both are rate-limiters. Shapers delay, policers drop or re-mark.
How many bits does the DSCP value use, and how many of the DS field's bits are left for ECN?
6 bits; 2 bits - 6 + 2 = 8 bits in the DS field.
Which two of these are Layer 3 QoS markings? CoS, DSCP, IP precedence, TID
DSCP and IP precedence - CoS is wired Layer 2; TID is wireless Layer 2.
Which DSCP value does voice normally use, and what is its PHB name?
46, EF (Expedited Forwarding) - EF gives strict priority with low loss, delay and jitter.
Name the problem when low-priority queues never get any bandwidth.
Starvation (caused by strict priority scheduling) - weighted methods avoid it.
Which QoS tool introduces jitter and delay but results in fewer TCP resends?
Shaping - it queues excess traffic instead of dropping it.
What is the difference between queuing and scheduling?
Queuing holds packets when the interface is congested; scheduling chooses which packet leaves next, always - queuing is activated by congestion, scheduling is not.
At what point in the network should traffic be marked, and why?
At the trust boundary (usually the edge switch), as close to the source as possible - so every later device can trust the marking.
What does LLQ add to CBWFQ?
A strict-priority queue for real-time traffic, giving a latency guarantee - without it, CBWFQ is only suited to data.
Which IP precedence value matches CS3, and what is the ToS byte for DSCP 24?
Which tool keeps important traffic from being dropped first when a queue starts to fill?
WRED - it drops lower-precedence traffic earlier.
In which direction (ingress or egress) is a policer usually placed, and why?
Ingress, because traffic that will be dropped anyway should be dropped as early as possible - shapers are usually placed on egress.
Gives different traffic different priority when a link is congested. Fights delay, drops, errors, jitter and out-of-order delivery.

Where markings stop being trusted and traffic is classified and marked. Usually the edge switch or an IP phone. Untrusted = PCs, printers.
CoS 3 bits (L2 wired, PCP). TID (L2 wireless). IP precedence 3 bits of ToS. DSCP 6 bits of the DS field (+2 ECN). L3 marking is end-to-end.
Default 0, CS3 24, AF41 34, EF 46 (voice). DSCP = 8x+2y for AFxy. ToS byte = DSCP x 4.
By markings, addressing (IP, ports) or application signatures (NBAR, most CPU). NBAR: passive (statistics) or active (classify for marking).
Both rate-limiters. Policer drops or re-marks, no delay, more TCP resends, ingress. Shaper delays, adds jitter, fewer resends, egress toward ISP.
Queuing only during congestion. Scheduling always. Strict priority can starve; round-robin hurts real-time; weighted fair is the better compromise.
FIFO, PQ (4 queues), CQ (16 queues), WFQ (by flow).
CBWFQ (bandwidth guarantees, data) and LLQ (CBWFQ + strict-priority queue, latency guarantee, voice).
Tail drop wastes bandwidth. TCP global synchronization wastes bandwidth. WRED drops early, weighted by priority.
